verdict.reasoning: Patient says, “I just feel I can't really hear as well as I used to, like my hearing is kind of deteriorating,” which indicates reduced hearing.

Duration: when asked how long, patient replies, “about six weeks.” Later, hearing loss is localized: “Uh just the left ear, yeah.” Intermittent nature is implied by overall intermittent symptom description and not contradicted.

Patient states, “I occasionally get like a ringing in my left ear… just on the one side” and later, “some things trigger it as well. So, for example, if I'm watching TV or listen to music or something that'll solve the ringing in the ear,” describing intermittent tinnitus in the left ear triggered by TV/music.

Patient reports, “there's actually been a few times when I felt kind of a bit sick or a bit dizzy as well” and clarifies, “nothing major… not the kind of dizziness you get with nausea, like uh not, not proper room spinning or anything like that but just, just a little bit kind of off balance,” which matches mild dizziness/off-balance without true vertigo or nausea.
Doctor asks, “have you had any pain from the ear at all?” and immediately follows with, “Uh no my left ear. Doctor: OK,” indicating the patient denies ear pain.
Doctor asks, “Any discharge coming out of the ear? No, OK,” documenting no ear discharge.
Doctor asks, “have you been experiencing any fever?” and the exchange continues without the doctor documenting a positive; the next line is “Right, OK,” consistent with no fever reported.
Doctor asks, “Have, have you had any chest pain with it?” Patient replies, “No.”
Doctor asks, “Any palpitations, heart beating fast?” and then says, “OK, fine, alright,” implying the patient did not report palpitations.

When asked if difficulty hearing is both ears or just the left, patient says, “Uh just the left ear, yeah.” Doctor responds, “Alright, so your right ear is fine,” indicating the right ear is unaffected.
Patient states, “Um I had something maybe, about a year ago, but it only lasted a couple of days,” describing a similar short episode about a year prior.
Doctor asks, “do you use cotton ball buds to try and clean out wax from your ears?” Patient replies, “Uh nah I'll do it,” which in context is a denial of using cotton buds.
Transcript documents left-sided decreased hearing (“just the left ear”), intermittent tinnitus in the left ear, and “a little bit kind of off balance,” consistent with mild disequilibrium.

Doctor mentions “Simple things might be wax… impacted wax, blocking the tube going into the eardrum,” and later, “It might be that there's a problem inside the drum or the balance system within the ear,” which covers cerumen impaction, middle ear pathology, and inner ear involvement.

Doctor states, “the first thing that we need to do is we need to get someone to have a look inside your ear… so we need to exclude that first… for that we need to have a look inside the ear drum,” describing the need for otoscopy to rule out obstruction.

Doctor labels the ringing as tinnitus: “The ringing that you got… it's something called Tinnitus,” and adds, “What I might do… I'm going to… paste the link for a leaflet about Tinnitus… I'd really appreciate it if you could start reading about it,” indicating patient education is planned.

Doctor says, “book you in for a face-to-face appointment in one of our clinics. It's not an emergency. It can be done within the next four, five days or so… one of the GPs will just have a quick look in the ear and figure out whether there's physical blockage or whether there's something else going on,” which is an otoscopic assessment for wax or middle ear issues in 4–5 days.
The transcript discusses identifying “impacted wax” as a possible cause but does not state a specific plan to remove cerumen “per clinic protocol” if found.
There is no mention in the transcript of audiometry, ENT referral, or a contingent plan if the ear exam is normal; only general discussion of possibilities and tinnitus information is provided.

Doctor states, “I'm going to… paste the link for a leaflet about Tinnitus, um, in the notes for this appointment. I'd really appreciate it if you could start reading about it,” matching provision of a tinnitus leaflet link and patient review.

Doctor says, “what I might do… I'll send a message to our admin team. I'll ask them to slot you into the clinic… Bear with me five minutes and then you can ring the support team, I'll leave the number in the notes for this appointment. Ring them, and then they'll slot you in,” which matches messaging admin and the patient calling the provided number.

Follow-up advice given is general: “If there's any problem, any issues between now and when the clinic appointment is, just book another appointment and you can speak to one of us over video,” without specific mention of worsening dizziness, ear pain, discharge, sudden hearing loss, neurological symptoms, chest pain, palpitations, or fever.
